sk: अथ हैनं कौसल्यश्चाश्वलायनः पप्रच्छ भगवन्कुत एष प्राणो जायते कथमायात्यस्मिञ्शरीरे आत्मानं वा प्रविभज्य कथं प्रतितिष्ठते केनोत्क्रमते कथं बाह्यमभिधत्ते कथमध्यात्ममिति ||
ro: atha · ha · enaṁ · kausalyaḥ · ca · āśvalāyanaḥ · papraccha · bhagavan · kutaḥ · eṣaḥ · prāṇaḥ · jāyate · katham · āyāti · asmin · śarīre · ātmānaṁ · vā · pravibhajya · kathaṁ · pratitiṣṭhate · kena · utkramate · kathaṁ · bāhyam · abhidhatte · katham · adhyātmam · iti ||
hi: तब कौसल्य आश्वलायन ने (पिप्पलाद से) पूछा — 'भगवन्! यह प्राण कहाँ से (kutaḥ) उत्पन्न होता है? इस शरीर में कैसे आता है? अपने आपको विभाजित करके कैसे प्रतिष्ठित होता है? किसके द्वारा (शरीर से) उत्क्रमण (बाहर निकलना) करता है? बाह्य (बाहरी जगत्) को कैसे धारण करता है? और अध्यात्म (आन्तरिक/शरीर) को कैसे (धारण करता है)?'
en: Then Kausalya Āshvalāyana asked him: 'Bhagavan! Whence (kutaḥ) is this Prāṇa born? How does it come into this body? How does it establish itself after dividing itself? By what does it depart? How does it sustain the external (bāhya)? And how the internal (adhyātma)?'

ws.e: Kausalya Āshvalāyana — the third questioner; from the Kushala lineage (kausalya) and the Āshvalāyana school (a śākhā of the Ṛg Veda)
whence / from what source — interrogative adverb; asks about the ultimate origin of Prāṇa
having divided — pra + vi + √bhaj (to divide); refers to the fivefold division of Prāṇa into prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna

ws.h: ऊपर उठकर जाता है / शरीर छोड़ता है
ws.e: departs / rises out — ut + √kram (to step); the departure of Prāṇa at death
the external — the outer world; how does Prāṇa relate to the macrocosm?
the internal / pertaining to the self — adhi + ātman; how does Prāṇa function within the body?

gr: Six sub-questions: Kausalya's question is the most methodical of all six — he asks six specific sub-questions: (1) kutaḥ jāyate — whence is it born? (origin); (2) katham āyāti — how does it come into the body? (entry); (3) ātmānaṁ pravibhajya kathaṁ pratitiṣṭhate — how does it establish itself after self-division? (fivefold differentiation); (4) kena utkramate — by what means does it depart? (death); (5) kathaṁ bāhyam abhidhatte — how does it sustain the external? (macrocosmic function); (6) katham adhyātmam — how does it sustain the internal? (microcosmic function). This systematic structure produces the most 'scientific' answer in the Prashna Upanishad — a complete physiology of the vital breath.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.1 — Question 3 deepens the Prāṇa-doctrine established in Questions 1-2. Question 1 asked about Prāṇa at the cosmic level (sun-moon, devayāna-pitṛyāṇa). Question 2 asked about Prāṇa's supremacy among the bodily devas. Question 3 now asks about Prāṇa's origin, mechanism, and operation — the most technical of the three. Kausalya's six sub-questions anticipate the structure of later Yoga texts (Yoga Sūtra, Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā) that systematically analyse prāṇa's origin, division, channels, and departure. The Āshvalāyana school (Kausalya's lineage) is one of the major śākhās of the Ṛg Veda.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — कौसल्य का प्रश्न प्राण के कारण (cause) को जानने के लिए है। प्रश्न 2 में प्राण की श्रेष्ठता सिद्ध हुई; अब प्रश्न है: यह श्रेष्ठ शक्ति कहाँ से आती है? उत्तर — आत्मा (ब्रह्म) से। यह अत्यन्त महत्त्वपूर्ण है क्योंकि इससे सिद्ध होगा कि प्राण स्वतंत्र तत्त्व नहीं, ब्रह्म का कार्य (effect) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Kausalya's question seeks the cause (kāraṇa) of Prāṇa. Question 2 established Prāṇa's supremacy; now the question is: where does this supreme power come from? The answer — from the Ātman (Brahman). This is crucial because it proves that Prāṇa is not an independent reality but an effect (kārya) of Brahman.
advaita.ins: You've proved Prāṇa is the mightiest power in the body. Good. But where does the mightiest power come from? If it's self-caused, it's Brahman. If it's caused by something else, then that something else is the real thing. This question cuts to the heart of the matter.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — छह उप-प्रश्न प्राण के सम्पूर्ण स्वरूप को जानने के लिए हैं — उत्पत्ति, प्रवेश, विभाजन, उत्क्रमण, बाह्य-कार्य, आध्यात्मिक-कार्य। यह भगवान् की शक्ति (vibhūti) का विस्तृत अध्ययन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the six sub-questions aim at knowing Prāṇa's complete nature — origin, entry, division, departure, external function, internal function. This is a detailed study of the Lord's power (vibhūti).
vishisht.ins: Six questions, one breath. Kausalya wants the complete manual — where it comes from, how it enters, how it works, how it leaves. He's asking for the engineering blueprint of life.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — कौसल्य का प्रश्न चेतना के अवतरण (descent of consciousness) की प्रक्रिया को जानने के लिए है। 'कुतः जायते' — चेतना का मूल स्रोत क्या है? 'कथम् आयाति' — वह शरीर में कैसे उतरती है? यह योग-विज्ञान का मूलभूत प्रश्न है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Kausalya's question seeks to understand the process of the descent of consciousness. 'Kutaḥ jāyate' — what is the original source of consciousness? 'Katham āyāti' — how does it descend into the body? This is the fundamental question of yoga-science.
aurobindo.ins: Before you can control the breath, you need to know where it comes from. Before you can redirect consciousness, you need to know how it entered. Kausalya's question is the yogi's first lesson.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is this the most 'scientific' question?
dp.a: Kausalya's question is structured like a scientific inquiry — it asks six precise sub-questions covering the complete lifecycle of Prāṇa: (1) Origin (kutaḥ jāyate): where does Prāṇa come from? What is its ultimate source? (2) Entry (katham āyāti): how does it enter a specific body? What is the mechanism of embodiment? (3) Differentiation (ātmānaṁ pravibhajya kathaṁ pratitiṣṭhate): how does one Prāṇa become five? What governs the division? (4) Departure (kena utkramate): what causes Prāṇa to leave? Through which channel does it depart? (5) External function (kathaṁ bāhyam abhidhatte): how does Prāṇa connect the individual to the external world? (6) Internal function (katham adhyātmam): how does it operate within the body? This systematic approach distinguishes Question 3 from the more philosophical Questions 1-2. The answer that follows (mantras 2-12) reads almost like a physiological treatise, describing channels (nāḍīs), energy centres, and the mechanisms of digestion, circulation, and death — making it a precursor to the detailed prāṇa-analysis in the Yoga Sūtra (2.49-53) and Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā.

dp.q: 🔍 How do the six questions in this Upanishad differ?
dp.a: Each of the six questions in the Prashna Upanishad addresses a different dimension of reality, progressively deepening: Q1 (Kabandhī): Cosmology — 'Whence are creatures born?' The macrocosmic level: Prāṇa and Rayi as cosmic duality. Q2 (Bhārgava): Physiology of consciousness — 'How many gods support a creature?' The microcosmic hierarchy: Prāṇa as supreme among bodily faculties. Q3 (Kausalya, this question): Mechanics of the vital force — 'Whence is Prāṇa born?' The technical details: origin, channels, division, departure. Q4 (Sauryāyaṇī): States of consciousness — 'What sleeps, what wakes?' The psychology: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. Q5 (Shaibya): Meditation — 'What is gained by meditating on OM?' The practice: technique and fruits of contemplation. Q6 (Sukesha): The Absolute — 'Where is the sixteen-part Person?' The metaphysics: the supreme Puruṣa and dissolution of the parts. The movement is from the outer (cosmos) to the inner (vital mechanics → consciousness → meditation → the Absolute). Question 3 is the pivot — it bridges the external (Q1-2) and the internal (Q4-6).

sk: तस्मै स होवाचातिप्रश्नान्पृच्छसि ब्रह्मिष्ठो ऽसीति तस्मात्ते ऽहं ब्रवीमि ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · atiprśnān · pṛcchasi · brahmiṣṭhaḥ · asi · iti · tasmāt · te · ahaṁ · bravīmi ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'तू अतिप्रश्न (अत्यन्त गूढ़/कठिन प्रश्न) पूछ रहा है। तू ब्रह्मिष्ठ (ब्रह्म में सर्वाधिक स्थित) है — इसलिए मैं तुझे (उत्तर) बताता हूँ।'
en: To him he (Pippalāda) said: 'You ask transcendent questions (atiprāśnān). You are most devoted to Brahman (brahmiṣṭha). Therefore I tell you.'

ws.e: transcendent questions / questions that go beyond — ati (beyond) + praśna (question); the questions exceed ordinary inquiry; they penetrate to the ultimate cause

ws.h: ब्रह्म में सर्वाधिक स्थित / ब्रह्म-ज्ञान में श्रेष्ठ
ws.e: most devoted to Brahman / most established in Brahman — superlative of brahmin (one who knows Brahman); the highest qualification a student can receive

gr: atiprśnān pṛcchasi — 'you ask questions that go beyond (ati)': Pippalāda acknowledges that this question surpasses the earlier two. Questions 1-2 asked about Prāṇa's effects (cosmological role, bodily supremacy); Question 3 asks about its cause — which is the deeper inquiry. brahmiṣṭhaḥ asi — 'you are brahmiṣṭha': the superlative form. Not just brahma-parā (devoted to Brahman, like the six seekers in 1.1) but brahmiṣṭha — the most devoted. This praise justifies why Pippalāda answers: only the most qualified student deserves the deepest teaching. tasmāt te ahaṁ bravīmi — 'therefore I tell you': the causal link is explicit — because you are brahmiṣṭha, therefore I teach. Knowledge is not withheld out of selfishness but released according to the student's readiness.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.2 — The guru's commendation of the student before answering is a standard Upanishadic motif. Compare Muṇḍaka 1.2.13: 'To that student who has duly approached, whose mind is calm, whose senses are controlled — to him the knowing teacher teaches the Brahma-vidyā.' The word atiprśna ('transcendent question') is unique to this Upanishad and signals that the answer will touch the deepest level — the origin of Prāṇa in Ātman itself.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मिष्ठ' — यह सर्वोच्च प्रशंसा है। गुरु केवल अधिकारी (qualified) शिष्य को ही गूढ़ ज्ञान देता है। 'अतिप्रश्न' — यह प्रश्न कार्य (effect) से कारण (cause) की ओर जाता है, जो विवेक (discrimination) का लक्षण है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'brahmiṣṭha' is the highest praise. The guru gives profound knowledge only to the qualified (adhikārī) student. 'Atiprśna' — this question moves from effect to cause, which is the mark of viveka (discrimination).
advaita.ins: The guru doesn't teach to impress. He teaches when the student is ready. 'You are brahmiṣṭha' isn't flattery — it's a diagnosis: you've done enough inner work that the answer won't destroy you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मिष्ठ' — कौसल्य की भगवद्-भक्ति उनके प्रश्न की गहराई से प्रकट होती है। जो भगवान् के बारे में गहरे प्रश्न पूछता है, वही सच्चा भक्त है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'brahmiṣṭha' — Kausalya's devotion to the Lord is revealed by the depth of his question. The one who asks deep questions about the Lord is the true devotee.
vishisht.ins: The best devotion isn't blind acceptance — it's deep questioning. Kausalya doesn't say 'I believe.' He says 'where does this come from?' That's the question of a devotee who wants to understand, not just worship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अतिप्रश्न' — यह प्रश्न चेतना के मूल स्रोत को छूता है। केवल वही पूछ सकता है जो स्वयं उस गहराई तक पहुँचने की तैयारी रखता हो। 'ब्रह्मिष्ठ' — चेतना में सर्वाधिक गहरे उतरा हुआ।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'atiprśna' — this question touches the very source of consciousness. Only one who is prepared to descend to that depth can ask it. 'Brahmiṣṭha' — the one who has gone deepest into consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: You can only ask a question if you're ready for the answer. The depth of your question reveals the depth of your preparation. Kausalya's question goes to the root — and Pippalāda recognises that he can handle the root-answer.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'atiprśna' (transcendent question) mean?
dp.a: The word atiprśna (अतिप्रश्न) — literally 'beyond-question' or 'transcendent question' — is unique to the Prashna Upanishad. It signals that Kausalya's inquiry exceeds ordinary philosophical discussion. Questions 1-2 asked about Prāṇa's effects: its cosmic role (Q1) and its bodily supremacy (Q2). These are observable and demonstrable. Question 3 asks about Prāṇa's cause — its ultimate origin. This is a fundamentally different type of inquiry because: (1) The cause of Prāṇa cannot be observed through the senses (you can feel breath but not its source). (2) The answer — 'from Ātman' — requires a leap from the physical to the metaphysical. (3) Understanding the origin of Prāṇa means understanding the origin of life itself — which is the deepest question any tradition can ask. The prefix ati- (beyond, across) is the same prefix in atīndriya (beyond the senses) and atīva (exceedingly). It marks this question as belonging to a higher order of inquiry.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the guru commend the student before answering?
dp.a: The guru's commendation of the student — brahmiṣṭho'si, 'you are the most devoted to Brahman' — before giving the teaching is a standard Upanishadic pattern. It appears in: Muṇḍaka 1.2.13: 'To that student who has duly approached, whose mind is calm, whose senses are controlled...' Kaṭha 1.2.13: Yama commends Nachiketa: 'You have rejected all pleasures; I consider you a worthy seeker.' Chāndogya 4.9.3: The fires commend Satyakāma: 'You are a truth-speaker; we will teach you.' The purpose is not flattery but adhikāra-nirṇaya — the determination of qualification. In the Vedic tradition, knowledge is not freely given to anyone; it is given to those who are ready. The commendation is the guru's public declaration that the student meets the prerequisites: tapas (austerity), brahmacarya (discipline), śraddhā (faith), and most importantly, viveka (the discrimination to ask the right question). Pippalāda's 'you are brahmiṣṭha' is not a compliment — it is a clearance.

sk: आत्मन एष प्राणो जायते यथैषा पुरुषे छायैतस्मिन्नेतदाततं मनोकृतेनायात्यस्मिञ्शरीरे ||
ro: ātmanaḥ · eṣaḥ · prāṇaḥ · jāyate · yathā · eṣā · puruṣe · chāyā · etasmin · etat · ātatam · mano-kṛtena · āyāti · asmin · śarīre ||
hi: आत्मा से यह प्राण उत्पन्न होता है। जैसे पुरुष (व्यक्ति) की छाया (shadow) होती है, वैसे ही यह (प्राण) इसमें (आत्मा में) आतत (फैला हुआ/विस्तृत) है। मनोकृतेन (मन के कर्म/संकल्प द्वारा) यह इस शरीर में आता है।
en: From the Ātman (Self) this Prāṇa is born. As a shadow belongs to a person, so this (Prāṇa) is extended (ātata) in this (Ātman). By the activity of mind (mano-kṛtena) it comes into this body.

ws.e: from the Ātman / from the Self — ablative; the ultimate source of Prāṇa is not matter or the elements but the Self (Ātman/Brahman)
shadow — Prāṇa is to the Ātman as a shadow is to the person who casts it: inseparable, dependent, yet not identical
extended / stretched — ā + √tan (to stretch); Prāṇa is 'stretched out' from the Ātman, like a shadow extending from a body
by the activity of mind — manas (mind) + kṛta (made/done); Prāṇa enters a specific body because of past mental impressions (karma/saṁskāra)

gr: ātmanaḥ eṣaḥ prāṇaḥ jāyate — 'from the Ātman this Prāṇa is born': the fundamental answer. Prāṇa does not arise from matter, from the elements, or from any external source — it arises from the Self. This establishes Ātman as the cause (kāraṇa) and Prāṇa as the effect (kārya). chāyā — the shadow-simile: just as a shadow is (1) inseparable from the person, (2) dependent on the person, and (3) not identical with the person — so Prāṇa is inseparable from Ātman, dependent on it, but not identical with it. The shadow has no independent existence. mano-kṛtena āyāti — 'by the activity of mind it comes into this body': this is the mechanism of rebirth. The mind's past karma (mental impressions, desires, saṁskāras) determines which body Prāṇa enters. The body is chosen not randomly but by the force of accumulated mental tendencies.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.3 — The declaration 'ātmanaḥ prāṇo jāyate' is one of the most important metaphysical statements in the Upanishads. Compare Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.20: 'As a spider sends forth and draws back (its thread), as herbs spring up on the earth... so from this Ātman all prāṇas proceed.' The shadow-simile (chāyā) is unique to the Prashna and provides a middle ground between identity (Prāṇa = Ātman) and total difference (Prāṇa ≠ Ātman). The 'mano-kṛtena' clause introduces the doctrine of karma — the mind's past actions determine embodiment — linking prāṇa-vidyā to karma-theory. Muṇḍaka 3.1.10 similarly states: 'Whatever world he fashions with his mind, that world he wins.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'आत्मनः प्राणो जायते' — प्राण ब्रह्म (आत्मा) से उत्पन्न होता है, जैसे छाया पुरुष से। छाया न तो पुरुष से भिन्न है, न अभिन्न — यही माया (illusion) का स्वरूप है। 'मनोकृतेन' — पूर्वजन्म के कर्म-संस्कार मन में रहते हैं; उन्हीं के कारण प्राण नए शरीर में प्रवेश करता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ātmanaḥ prāṇo jāyate' — Prāṇa is born from Brahman (Ātman), like a shadow from a person. The shadow is neither identical with nor different from the person — this is the nature of māyā. 'Mano-kṛtena' — the karma-saṁskāras (impressions) of past lives reside in the mind; because of these, Prāṇa enters a new body.
advaita.ins: Your shadow doesn't have a life of its own. It doesn't decide where to go. It follows you — completely dependent, yet appearing to be separate. That's the relationship between Prāṇa and the Ātman. The breath in your body is the Self's shadow — and you're living in the shadow, thinking it's the real thing.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'आत्मनः जायते' — प्राण ईश्वर (परमात्मा) से उत्पन्न होता है, किन्तु 'उत्पत्ति' का अर्थ 'रूपान्तरण' (transformation) नहीं, 'अभिव्यक्ति' (manifestation) है। छाया-उपमा — प्राण ईश्वर का शरीर (body) है; शरीर आत्मा से अभिन्न और आश्रित (dependent) होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'ātmanaḥ jāyate' — Prāṇa is born from the Lord (Paramātman), but 'born' means 'manifested', not 'transformed'. The shadow-simile: Prāṇa is the Lord's body (śarīra); a body is inseparable from and dependent on the soul.
vishisht.ins: Your breath is the Lord's shadow — not a piece broken off, but a projection that can't exist without the original. It manifests from Him like a shadow from a form. Pull the form away and the shadow vanishes.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'आत्मनः प्राणो जायते' — प्राण (जीवन-शक्ति) चेतना (consciousness) से उत्पन्न होती है, पदार्थ (matter) से नहीं। यह भौतिकवाद (materialism) का प्रत्यक्ष खण्डन है। 'मनोकृतेन' — मन का संकल्प (will) ही शरीर-निर्माण का कारण है — यह चेतना के शरीर पर आधिपत्य का प्रमाण है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'ātmanaḥ prāṇo jāyate' — the life-force (prāṇa) is born from consciousness (ātman), not from matter. This is a direct refutation of materialism. 'Mano-kṛtena' — the mind's will (saṅkalpa) is the cause of body-formation — proof that consciousness governs matter, not the reverse.
aurobindo.ins: Life doesn't emerge from dead matter. Consciousness doesn't arise from chemistry. The Upanishad says the opposite: Prāṇa comes from Ātman. Life is a projection of the spirit, not an accident of the molecule.

dp.q: 🔍 What does the shadow (chāyā) simile teach?
dp.a: The shadow simile is one of the most philosophically precise analogies in the Upanishads. It teaches the relationship between Ātman and Prāṇa through five key properties of shadows: (1) Dependence: a shadow cannot exist without the person who casts it. Similarly, Prāṇa cannot exist without Ātman. Remove the Self, and the vital force vanishes. (2) Inseparability: wherever the person goes, the shadow follows. Ātman and Prāṇa are never found apart — wherever there is a Self, there is life. (3) Non-identity: the shadow is not the person. You can step on a shadow without hurting the person. Similarly, Prāṇa is not the Ātman — the vital force can be disturbed (illness, injury) without the Ātman being affected. (4) Derivation: the shadow derives its shape from the person. Similarly, Prāṇa's characteristics derive from the Ātman — it is conscious because the Ātman is conscious, it is active because the Ātman is active. (5) Insubstantiality: a shadow has no substance of its own — it is a play of light and form. Similarly, Prāṇa has no independent reality; it is a 'play' of the Ātman in the body. For Advaita, this simile is crucial: it positions Prāṇa as vivarta (apparent transformation), not pariṇāma (real transformation) — the Ātman doesn't actually change into Prāṇa; it merely appears to, like a person appearing to have a shadow.

dp.q: 🔍 How does 'mano-kṛtena' explain rebirth?
dp.a: The phrase mano-kṛtena āyāti asmin śarīre ('by the mind's activity it comes into this body') is the Upanishadic explanation of how rebirth works. The mechanism: (1) During life: the mind generates saṁskāras (impressions) through every thought, desire, and action. These saṁskāras accumulate as the mind's karma-residue. (2) At death: the gross body (sthūla-śarīra) disintegrates, but the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra) — composed of the mind, prāṇas, and saṁskāras — departs through one of the nāḍīs (channels). (3) Between lives: the mind's accumulated tendencies (vāsanās) determine which body Prāṇa will next enter — 'mano-kṛtena' ('by the mind's making'). (4) At rebirth: Prāṇa enters a new body shaped by the mind's past activities. The body is not randomly assigned — it is mano-kṛta (mind-made). This doctrine appears across the Upanishads: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.5: 'As is one's desire, so is one's will; as is one's will, so is one's deed; as is one's deed, so is what one attains.' Chāndogya 3.14.1: 'Man is a creature of will (kratu). As he wills in this world, so does he become after death.' The mind is the architect of the next body. This is why the Upanishads emphasise manas-śuddhi (purification of the mind) — a pure mind leads to liberation; an impure mind leads to continued rebirth.

ro: yathā · samrāṭ · eva · adhikṛtān · viniyuṅkte · etān · grāmān · etān · grāmān · adhitiṣṭhasva · iti · evam · eva · eṣaḥ · prāṇaḥ · itarān · prāṇān · pṛthak · pṛthak · eva · sannidhatte ||
hi: जैसे सम्राट् (चक्रवर्ती राजा) अधिकारियों (अधिकृतान्) को नियुक्त करता है — 'इन ग्रामों पर तू अधिकार कर, इन ग्रामों पर तू' — वैसे ही यह प्राण अन्य प्राणों (apāna, vyāna आदि) को पृथक्-पृथक् (अलग-अलग स्थानों पर) नियुक्त (सन्निधत्ते) करता है।
en: Just as an emperor (samrāṭ) appoints officers — 'Govern these villages, govern those villages' — so this Prāṇa stations the other vital breaths (itarān prāṇān), each in its own separate place (pṛthak pṛthak).

ws.e: emperor / sovereign ruler — sam (together) + rāj (to rule); the supreme ruler who delegates authority to subordinate officers
appointed officers — adhi + √kṛ (to do/appoint); officials who govern on behalf of the emperor

ws.h: नियुक्त करता है / अलग-अलग काम सौंपता है
ws.e: appoints / assigns — vi + ni + √yuj (to yoke); the emperor 'yokes' each officer to a specific set of villages
separately, each in its own place — the reduplication emphasises that each prāṇa has its own distinct domain

ws.h: स्थापित करता है / नियुक्त करता है
ws.e: stations / places — sam + ni + √dhā (to place); Prāṇa places each sub-prāṇa in its assigned region of the body

gr: samrāṭ — 'emperor': not merely a rājan (king) but a samrāṭ (sovereign over many kingdoms). This is the highest political title in Vedic literature. The metaphor says Prāṇa is not just a chief among equals (like a rājan) but an absolute sovereign (samrāṭ) whose authority is unquestionable. grāmān adhitiṣṭhasva — 'govern these villages': each sub-prāṇa is assigned a 'territory' (a region of the body) and told to govern it. This establishes a political metaphor for bodily physiology: the body is an empire, Prāṇa is the emperor, and the five sub-prāṇas are provincial governors. pṛthak pṛthak — the doubling of 'separately' emphasises that the five prāṇas occupy distinct regions — they are not mixed or interchangeable. The following mantras will specify each territory.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.4 — The political metaphor (samrāṭ appointing officers) is unique to the Prashna Upanishad. Other Upanishads describe the five prāṇas but don't use this administrative analogy. The metaphor has practical significance: just as an emperor's officers must stay in their assigned regions, each prāṇa must remain in its proper zone for the body to function. When a prāṇa moves out of its territory (e.g., apāna rising instead of descending), disease results — a principle foundational to Āyurveda. The five prāṇas and their territories are detailed in mantras 5-7.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सम्राट्-उपमा यह दिखाती है कि प्राण (मुख्य प्राण) एक (eka) है; अपान, व्यान आदि उसके 'अधिकारी' (delegates) हैं। जैसे अधिकारी सम्राट् के बिना शक्तिहीन हैं, वैसे ही उप-प्राण मुख्य प्राण के बिना निष्क्रिय हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says the emperor-simile shows that Prāṇa (the chief breath) is one (eka); apāna, vyāna, etc. are its delegates. Just as officers are powerless without the emperor, the sub-prāṇas are inert without the chief Prāṇa.
advaita.ins: One emperor, five governors. The governors think they run their provinces independently. But remove the emperor, and their authority vanishes overnight. The five breaths work the same way — they function only because the one Prāṇa empowers them.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सम्राट्-उपमा ईश्वर के शासन (governance) को दर्शाती है। भगवान् (प्राण-रूप में) प्रत्येक शक्ति को उसका कर्तव्य-क्षेत्र (assigned domain) देते हैं। शरीर ईश्वर का राज्य है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the emperor-simile illustrates the Lord's governance. The Lord (in the form of Prāṇa) assigns each power its domain. The body is the Lord's kingdom.
vishisht.ins: Your body is a well-governed empire. The emperor (Prāṇa/Lord) doesn't do every job — He delegates. But every governor's authority traces back to one throne.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण एक केन्द्रीय चेतना-शक्ति है जो विभिन्न कार्यों के लिए अपने आपको विभाजित करती है — यह चेतना की 'विशेषीकरण' (specialisation) की प्रक्रिया है। प्रत्येक उप-प्राण एक विशिष्ट कार्य (function) में विशेषज्ञ (specialised) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Prāṇa is a central consciousness-force that divides itself for different functions — this is the process of consciousness's 'specialisation'. Each sub-prāṇa is specialised for a specific function.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness doesn't descend into the body as one monolithic block. It specialises — one current for breathing, one for digesting, one for circulating, one for ascending, one for excreting. Same force, five specialists.

dp.q: 🔍 Why use a political metaphor for the body?
dp.a: The samrāṭ (emperor) metaphor is one of the Prashna Upanishad's most original contributions. It treats the body as a political system: an empire with a sovereign (Prāṇa), provincial governors (the five sub-prāṇas), and assigned territories (body regions). This metaphor works on several levels: (1) Hierarchy: just as an emperor outranks all officers, the chief Prāṇa outranks all sub-prāṇas. This was proved in Question 2 (the departure-test). (2) Delegation: the emperor doesn't govern every village personally — he delegates. Similarly, Prāṇa doesn't perform every bodily function directly — it assigns specific functions to apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna. (3) Order: when officers stay in their assigned territories, the empire prospers. When they overstep, chaos results. Similarly, when each prāṇa operates in its proper zone, health results. When they move out of position, disease follows — a principle that became foundational to Āyurveda. (4) Single authority: multiple officers, one sovereign. Multiple functions, one life-force. The political metaphor teaches unity-in-diversity: the body's many functions are not independent systems but expressions of one sovereign power.

dp.q: 🔍 The five prāṇas and their 'territories'
dp.a: The emperor assigns five governors to five regions. The traditional territories of the five prāṇas are: (1) Prāṇa (capital-P) — governs the region from the nose to the heart. Functions: inhalation, swallowing, sensory intake. Direction: forward and upward. (2) Apāna — governs the region below the navel, specifically the organs of excretion and reproduction. Functions: excretion, urination, reproduction, downward-moving energy. Direction: downward. (3) Samāna — governs the navel region (the digestive fire zone). Functions: digestion, assimilation, equal distribution of nutrients. Direction: inward/centralising. (4) Udāna — governs the throat and head. Functions: speech, effort, vomiting, and the departure of the soul at death. Direction: upward. (5) Vyāna — pervades the entire body; it has no single seat. Functions: circulation of blood and nutrients through the nāḍīs (channels), movement of limbs. Direction: outward/diffusing. This fivefold division is foundational to Yoga (prāṇāyāma works by controlling these five) and Āyurveda (vāta-doṣa is classified by which prāṇa is disturbed).

sk: पायूपस्थे ऽपानं चक्षुःश्रोत्रे मुखनासिकाभ्यां प्राणः स्वयं प्रतिष्ठते मध्ये तु समानः एष ह्येतद्धुतमन्नं समं नयति तस्मादेताः सप्तार्चिषो भवन्ति ||
ro: pāyu-upasthe · apānaṁ · cakṣuḥ-śrotre · mukha-nāsikābhyāṁ · prāṇaḥ · svayaṁ · pratitiṣṭhate · madhye · tu · samānaḥ · eṣaḥ · hi · etat · hutam · annaṁ · samaṁ · nayati · tasmāt · etāḥ · sapta · arciṣaḥ · bhavanti ||
hi: पायु (गुदा) और उपस्थ (जननेन्द्रिय) में अपान (स्थित है)। चक्षु (नेत्र), श्रोत्र (कान), मुख (मुँह), और नासिका (नाक) में प्राण स्वयं प्रतिष्ठित है। मध्य (बीच/नाभि-प्रदेश) में समान है — यह (समान) इस हुत (अर्पित/खाए हुए) अन्न को समान रूप से (सम) वितरित करता है। इसीलिए (जठराग्नि की) ये सात अर्चियाँ (ज्वालाएँ/लपटें) होती हैं।
en: In the organs of excretion (pāyu) and generation (upastha), apāna (is stationed). In the eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils, Prāṇa itself is established. In the middle, samāna — for it distributes equally (sama) the food that has been offered (huta). From this (digestive fire) arise the seven flames (sapta arciṣaḥ).

ws.e: the organ of excretion — the anus; one of apāna's two territories
the organ of generation — the reproductive organ; apāna's second territory; apāna governs both elimination and reproduction

ws.h: समान वायु / समान रूप से वितरण करने वाला प्राण
ws.e: samāna — the 'equalising' breath; seated in the middle (navel region); its function is to distribute digested food equally throughout the body

ws.h: हवन किया हुआ / अर्पित / खाया हुआ
ws.e: offered / sacrificed — from √hu (to offer into fire); eating is treated as a homa (fire-offering) into the digestive fire
seven flames — the seven tongues of the digestive fire; traditionally identified with the two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and the mouth — the seven openings of the head through which Prāṇa operates

gr: Three territories assigned: (1) Apāna → pāyu and upastha (lower body); (2) Prāṇa → eyes, ears, mouth, nostrils (head region); (3) Samāna → the middle (navel/digestive zone). This is the spatial assignment the emperor-simile (mantra 4) promised. svayaṁ pratitiṣṭhate — 'itself is established': the chief Prāṇa personally governs the head region — the most important territory (the seat of consciousness). It doesn't delegate this to a sub-prāṇa. hutam annam samaṁ nayati — 'distributes the offered food equally': the word huta treats eating as a fire-sacrifice — food is 'offered' into the jāṭharāgni (digestive fire). Samāna's job is equal distribution (sama + √nī). sapta arciṣaḥ — 'seven flames': the seven openings of the head (2 eyes + 2 ears + 2 nostrils + 1 mouth = 7) through which Prāṇa's fire manifests — seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting are all 'flames' of the vital fire.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.5 — The assignment of territories matches the standard Vedāntic-Āyurvedic schema. The 'seven flames' (sapta arciṣaḥ) are the seven head-openings — this corresponds to the Muṇḍaka (1.2.4) description of the seven tongues of the sacrificial fire (Kālī, Karālī, etc.), here internalized as the seven sensory openings. The Chāndogya (5.18-24) describes the prāṇāgnihotra (offering into the five prāṇas), and the Maitri Upanishad (2.6) explicitly maps the seven prāṇas to the seven flames. The locative constructions (pāyu-upasthe, cakṣuḥ-śrotre) precisely locate each prāṇa in its anatomical zone.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — तीन प्रमुख प्राणों के क्षेत्र: अपान = अधोभाग (lower body), प्राण = शिरोभाग (head), समान = मध्यभाग (middle)। यह शरीर को तीन खण्डों में विभाजित करता है। 'सप्त अर्चिषः' — शिर के सात छिद्र (openings) प्राण की सात ज्वालाएँ हैं — ये इन्द्रियज्ञान (sensory knowledge) के द्वार हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says the three main prāṇas divide the body into three zones: apāna = lower, prāṇa = upper (head), samāna = middle. 'Seven flames' — the seven head-openings are seven flames of Prāṇa — they are the gates of sensory knowledge.
advaita.ins: Your body has three floors: the basement (apāna handles elimination), the ground floor (samāna handles digestion and distribution), and the penthouse (prāṇa handles the senses). Seven windows on top let the light in.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण के तीन क्षेत्र भगवान् की शरीर-शासन-व्यवस्था (body-governance) को दर्शाते हैं। 'हुतम् अन्नम्' — भोजन एक यज्ञ है जिसमें समान-वायु अग्नि है। भगवान् ने शरीर को एक सुव्यवस्थित यंत्र (machine) बनाया है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the three zones of Prāṇa reflect the Lord's body-governance system. 'Hutam annam' — food is a sacrifice in which samāna is the fire. The Lord has made the body a well-organised machine.
vishisht.ins: The body is the Lord's most intricate machine. Three zones, five governors, seven flame-outlets. Every meal is a sacrifice, every breath a prayer. The engineering is divine — literally.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन क्षेत्र चेतना के तीन स्तर हैं: अपान = भौतिक/अवचेतन (subconscient), समान = प्राणिक/जीवन-स्तर (vital), प्राण = मानसिक/चेतन (mental-conscious)। 'सात ज्वालाएँ' — चेतना के सात द्वार जिनसे बाह्य जगत् का अनुभव होता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the three zones are three levels of consciousness: apāna = the physical/subconscient, samāna = the vital/life-level, prāṇa = the mental/conscious. 'Seven flames' — seven doors of consciousness through which the external world is experienced.
aurobindo.ins: Three levels, not just three body-zones. Below: the subconscient processes you never see (elimination, reproduction). Middle: the vital processes you half-see (digestion, assimilation). Above: the conscious processes you see (sight, sound, speech). The seven flames are your seven windows on the world.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the 'seven flames' (sapta arciṣaḥ)?
dp.a: The seven flames (sapta arciṣaḥ) are the seven openings of the head: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and one mouth (2+2+2+1 = 7). These are called 'flames' because: (1) Each is a sensory fire that 'burns' incoming stimuli into conscious perception — sight converts light into vision, hearing converts vibrations into sound, etc. (2) The Muṇḍaka Upanishad (1.2.4) names seven tongues of the sacrificial fire: Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, Viśvarūpī. In the Prashna's internalised version, these seven tongues become the seven sensory openings. (3) In Āyurveda, the concept of dhātu-agni (tissue-fire) is related: each dhātu (tissue) has its own metabolic fire. The seven head-openings are the most visible sites where the body's internal fire meets the external world. The connection to digestion is made explicit: samāna distributes digested food, and the energy from that food fuels the seven sensory fires. Thus eating → digestion → distribution → sensory consciousness forms a single chain.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Āyurveda use the five-prāṇa model?
dp.a: The five-prāṇa model described in this mantra became the foundation of Āyurvedic physiology: Prāṇa-vāyu (in the head): governs inhalation, swallowing, sneezing, and belching. Disorders: hiccups, asthma, respiratory problems. Apāna-vāyu (below the navel): governs defecation, urination, menstruation, childbirth, and ejaculation. Disorders: constipation, urinary problems, menstrual irregularities. Samāna-vāyu (navel region): governs digestion (agni), absorption, and nutrient distribution. Disorders: indigestion, malabsorption, metabolic imbalance. Udāna-vāyu (throat): governs speech, effort, memory, and vomiting. Disorders: speech problems, thyroid issues, loss of voice. Vyāna-vāyu (whole body): governs circulation, muscular movement, and joint function. Disorders: poor circulation, tremors, joint problems. In Āyurvedic diagnosis, the physician determines which prāṇa is vitiated (moved out of its territory) and prescribes treatment to return it to its seat — exactly as the emperor-simile suggests: health is when each governor stays in his assigned region.

sk: हृदि ह्येष आत्मा अत्रैतदेकशतं नाडीनां तासां शतं शतमेकैकस्या द्वासप्ततिर्द्वासप्ततिः प्रतिशाखानाडीसहस्राणि भवन्त्यासु व्यानश्चरति ||
ro: hṛdi · hi · eṣaḥ · ātmā · atra · etat · ekaśataṁ · nāḍīnāṁ · tāsāṁ · śataṁ · śatam · ekaikasyāḥ · dvāsaptatir · dvāsaptatiḥ · pratiśākhā-nāḍī-sahasrāṇi · bhavanti · āsu · vyānaḥ · carati ||
hi: हृदय में ही यह आत्मा (निवास करता) है। यहाँ एक सौ एक (101) नाडियाँ हैं। उनमें से प्रत्येक की सौ-सौ (100) शाखाएँ हैं। प्रत्येक शाखा की बहत्तर-बहत्तर हज़ार (72,000) प्रतिशाखा-नाडियाँ हैं। इनमें व्यान विचरण करता है।
en: In the heart (hṛdi) indeed is this Ātman. Here are one hundred and one (101) channels (nāḍīs). Each of these has one hundred branches. Each branch has seventy-two thousand sub-branches (pratiśākhā-nāḍī-sahasrāṇi). In these, vyāna moves.

ws.e: in the heart — the heart-cave (hṛd-guha) is the seat of the Ātman in Upanishadic thought; not merely the physical heart but the spiritual centre of the body
one hundred and one — the traditional count of principal nāḍīs; 101 major channels radiate from the heart
of the channels — nāḍī (from √nad, to flow); subtle energy channels through which prāṇa circulates; not identical with physical nerves or blood vessels
sub-branches — prati (each) + śākhā (branch); the finest capillary-like channels of the subtle body
vyāna — the 'pervading' breath; it circulates through all the nāḍīs, carrying nutrients and energy to every part of the body

gr: hṛdi ātmā — 'in the heart is the Self': the heart (hṛd) is the seat of the Ātman. This is stated across the Upanishads: Kaṭha 2.1.1 ('the Self, the size of a thumb, dwells in the heart'), Chāndogya 8.1.1 ('within the city of Brahman — the body — is a small lotus, the heart'). ekaśatam nāḍīnām — '101 nāḍīs': 101 principal channels radiate from the heart. The Chāndogya (8.6.6) and Kaṭha (2.3.16) also cite this number. The branching calculation: 101 × 100 × 72,000 = 727,200,000 sub-channels. This astronomical number symbolises the prāṇa's reach into every cell of the body. The exact figure is not meant as a literal count but as an expression of totality: Prāṇa reaches everywhere. vyānaḥ carati — 'vyāna moves (in these)': vyāna is the prāṇa assigned to the entire nāḍī system — the circulatory breath that pervades every channel.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.6 — The 101 nāḍīs are cited in Chāndogya 8.6.6, Kaṭha 2.3.16, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.2.3. The branching structure (101 → 100 each → 72,000 each) gives 727,200,000 total sub-channels — this anticipates the later Yoga tradition's standard count of 72,000 nāḍīs (which actually refers to the sub-branches per main branch, not the total). The three most important nāḍīs (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā) are not named here but are implied — suṣumnā appears in the next mantra as the channel of udāna. The Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (3.1-5) elaborates this system extensively.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'हृदि आत्मा' — आत्मा का स्थान हृदय-गुहा (heart-cave) है। 101 नाडियाँ सूक्ष्म शरीर (subtle body) की हैं, स्थूल शरीर की नहीं। व्यान सम्पूर्ण शरीर में प्राण-शक्ति का संचार करता है — यह आत्मा की सर्वव्यापकता का शारीरिक प्रतिबिम्ब है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'hṛdi ātmā' — the Self is seated in the heart-cave. The 101 nāḍīs belong to the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), not the gross body. Vyāna circulates prāṇa-energy throughout the body — this is the bodily reflection of the Ātman's omnipresence.
advaita.ins: 101 main channels, hundreds of millions of sub-channels. The Ātman sits at the centre of this network like a spider at the centre of its web. Every thread vibrates with the spider's life. That's vyāna — the breath that reaches everywhere.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'हृदि आत्मा' — जीवात्मा (individual self) भगवान् के साथ हृदय में निवास करता है। 101 नाडियाँ भगवान् की सृष्टि-व्यवस्था (creation-design) हैं — शरीर के प्रत्येक कण तक प्राण पहुँचाने के लिए।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'hṛdi ātmā' — the individual self (jīvātman) dwells in the heart along with the Lord. The 101 nāḍīs are the Lord's design — ensuring Prāṇa reaches every particle of the body.
vishisht.ins: The Lord didn't just put life in the body and leave. He built 727 million channels to make sure that life reaches every single cell. That's the depth of divine engineering.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'हृदि आत्मा' — हृदय चेतना का केन्द्र (centre of consciousness) है, मस्तिष्क नहीं। नाडी-तंत्र (nāḍī-system) चेतना के प्रवाह-मार्ग (channels of consciousness) हैं — ये स्थूल तंत्रिकाओं (nerves) से सूक्ष्मतर (subtler) हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'hṛdi ātmā' — the heart is the centre of consciousness, not the brain. The nāḍī-system comprises channels of consciousness — subtler than the physical nervous system.
aurobindo.ins: The brain processes information. The heart houses consciousness. These channels aren't nerves — they're pathways of awareness. When yogis speak of 'opening the heart', this is what they mean: clearing the 101 channels so consciousness can flow unobstructed.

dp.q: 🔍 What are nāḍīs?
dp.a: The nāḍīs (नाड़ी, from √nad, 'to flow') are subtle energy channels through which prāṇa (life-force) circulates in the body. They are not identical with physical structures like nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic channels — though there is functional overlap. Key points: Number: The Upanishads cite 101 principal nāḍīs (Praśna, Kaṭha, Chāndogya). Later Yoga texts (Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā) standardise the sub-branch count at 72,000. Origin: All nāḍīs radiate from the heart (hṛd-padma, the heart-lotus). Three principal nāḍīs: (1) Suṣumnā — the central channel, running from the base of the spine to the crown of the head. The channel of spiritual ascent. (2) Iḍā — the left channel, associated with the moon, cooling energy, and the parasympathetic nervous system. (3) Piṅgalā — the right channel, associated with the sun, heating energy, and the sympathetic nervous system. Function: vyāna circulates through the entire nāḍī network, distributing nutrients and consciousness. When nāḍīs are blocked (by physical or mental impurities), prāṇa cannot flow freely — this causes disease. Yoga's goal: nāḍī-śodhana (channel-purification) through prāṇāyāma, so that prāṇa can enter the suṣumnā and ascend to higher states of consciousness.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the heart (not the brain) the seat of the Self?
dp.a: The Upanishads consistently place the Ātman in the heart (hṛd-guha, 'heart-cave'), not in the brain. This is not anatomical ignorance — the Vedic tradition knew the brain existed — but a deliberate philosophical and yogic claim: (1) Experiential basis: meditators report that deep states of consciousness are 'felt' in the chest, not the head. The heart-centre (hṛd-padma) is the locus of the anāhata chakra in Yoga — the point where the individual self is experienced. (2) Philosophical reason: the brain is an organ of processing (it computes), but the heart is the seat of being (it is). Consciousness as awareness is located in the heart; consciousness as thought is located in the brain. The Upanishads are interested in awareness, not thought. (3) Textual consistency: Kaṭha 2.1.1: 'The Self, the size of a thumb, dwells in the heart.' Chāndogya 8.1.1: 'Within the body is a lotus called the heart; within that is a small space — as great as this universe.' Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.17: 'The Self rests in the heart.' (4) Practical consequence: in meditation, one is instructed to focus on the heart-centre (hṛd-dhyāna), not the brain. Ramana Maharshi taught that self-enquiry ('Who am I?') naturally draws attention to the right side of the chest — the spiritual heart (hṛdayam).

sk: अथैकयोर्ध्व उदानः पुण्येन पुण्यं लोकं नयति पापेन पापमुभाभ्यामेव मनुष्यलोकम् ||
ro: atha · ekayā · ūrdhvaḥ · udānaḥ · puṇyena · puṇyaṁ · lokaṁ · nayati · pāpena · pāpam · ubhābhyām · eva · manuṣya-lokam ||
hi: और एक (नाडी) से ऊर्ध्व (ऊपर) उदान (ले जाता है) — पुण्य (सत्कर्म) से पुण्य-लोक में, पाप (दुष्कर्म) से पाप-लोक में, और दोनों (पुण्य-पाप) के मिश्रण से मनुष्य-लोक में (ले जाता है)।
en: Then, through one (nāḍī), upward (ūrdhva), udāna leads — by merit (puṇya) to the meritorious world, by sin (pāpa) to the sinful world, and by both (ubhābhyām) to the human world (manuṣya-loka).

ws.e: by one (channel) — refers to the suṣumnā nāḍī, the central channel through which udāna ascends at death; the specific channel determines the destination
upward — udāna's defining direction is upward; at death, it draws the vital force upward through the crown

ws.h: उदान वायु / ऊपर ले जाने वाला प्राण
ws.e: udāna — the 'upward-moving' breath; governs departure at death, speech, and effort; its direction determines which world the soul reaches
the meritorious world — deva-loka (heaven); attained through accumulated good karma
the human world — rebirth as a human being; the result of a mixture of puṇya and pāpa

gr: ekayā ūrdhvaḥ — 'through one (nāḍī), upward': the one nāḍī is the suṣumnā — the central channel that runs from the heart to the crown of the head (brahma-randhra). At death, udāna draws the life-force upward through this channel. Three destinations based on karma: (1) puṇya → puṇya-loka (heaven/deva-loka); (2) pāpa → pāpa-loka (lower realms/naraka); (3) mixture of both → manuṣya-loka (human rebirth). This is the most concise statement of the karma-rebirth mechanism in the Upanishads. The role of udāna: udāna is the 'transporter' at death. It doesn't judge — it simply carries the jīva to the destination determined by the accumulated karma. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.2) describes this in more detail: 'The tip of the heart lights up; by that light the Self departs, either through the eye, or the head, or other parts of the body.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.7 — The three-destination scheme (puṇya-loka, pāpa-loka, manuṣya-loka) is a simplified version of the five-fire / two-path doctrine found in Chāndogya 5.3-10 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2. In those longer accounts, the virtuous go by the devayāna (path of the gods, no return) and the ritualists by the pitṛyāṇa (path of the fathers, return to rebirth). The Prashna simplifies this to three outcomes based on karma-balance. The identification of the 'one nāḍī' (ekayā) with suṣumnā is confirmed by Kaṭha 2.3.16: 'One of these (101 nāḍīs) goes upward through the head; by that one goes to immortality.' The Haṭha Yoga tradition later made suṣumnā the central goal of practice.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — उदान कर्मफल (fruits of karma) के अनुसार जीव को ऊपर ले जाता है। किन्तु ज्ञानी (knower of Brahman) के लिए कोई लोक-गमन नहीं — वह मुक्त हो जाता है; उसका प्राण ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (crown) से निकलकर ब्रह्म में विलीन हो जाता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says udāna carries the jīva upward according to karma-fruits. But for the knower of Brahman (jñānī), there is no travel to any world — he is liberated; his prāṇa exits through the brahma-randhra (crown) and merges into Brahman.
advaita.ins: Three tickets, three destinations: heaven for the virtuous, hell for the wicked, earth for the mixed. But there's a fourth option the mantra doesn't mention: no ticket needed. The knower doesn't travel anywhere — he was already home.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — उदान भगवान् का न्याय-दूत (messenger of justice) है। कर्मानुसार जीव को उचित लोक में ले जाना — यह ईश्वरीय न्याय (divine justice) है। भक्त को भगवान् स्वयं उत्तम लोक (paramam padam) में ले जाते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says udāna is the Lord's messenger of justice. Carrying the jīva to the appropriate world based on karma is divine justice. The devotee is personally taken by the Lord to the supreme abode (paramam padam).
vishisht.ins: Karma is the Lord's accounting system. Udāna is the courier. You packed the bag during your life — merit and sin — and udāna delivers you to the destination your bag indicates. Only the devotee travels with the Lord's personal escort.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — उदान मृत्यु के समय चेतना को ऊपर खींचता है। चेतना का स्तर (level of consciousness) निर्धारित करता है कि जीव कहाँ जाता है। पुण्य-पाप = चेतना की गुणवत्ता (quality), न कि कर्मकाण्डीय हिसाब।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says udāna draws consciousness upward at death. The level of consciousness determines where the jīva goes. Puṇya-pāpa = the quality of consciousness, not a ritualistic accounting.
aurobindo.ins: Your destination after death isn't decided by a ledger of good and bad deeds. It's decided by the quality of consciousness you've built during life. Merit and sin are just names for the grade of awareness you've cultivated.

dp.q: 🔍 How does udāna determine the afterlife destination?
dp.a: The mantra describes a precise mechanism of post-mortem transit: Step 1: At death, the sub-prāṇas withdraw from their territories and converge on the chief Prāṇa in the heart. Step 2: Udāna (the upward-moving breath) then draws the life-force upward through one of the 101 nāḍīs — specifically the suṣumnā, the central channel. Step 3: The karmic load (the accumulated puṇya and pāpa) determines the exit-point and destination: Puṇya-dominant → exits through the upper openings (crown, eyes) → ascends to deva-loka (heaven). Pāpa-dominant → exits through the lower openings → descends to lower realms. Mixed (puṇya + pāpa) → returns to manuṣya-loka (human rebirth). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.1-2) elaborates: 'The tip of the heart lights up; by that light the Self departs. When it departs through the eye, that is liberation; when through the head, that is heaven...' The Kaṭha (2.3.16) adds: 'One of the 101 nāḍīs goes to the crown; by that one goes to immortality. The others lead to various departures.' The practical implication: yoga prepares the suṣumnā so that at death, udāna can carry consciousness straight upward to liberation, bypassing the karma-determined detours.

dp.q: 🔍 The three lokas and the karma balance
dp.a: The Prashna's three-destination scheme is the simplest version of the Upanishadic afterlife doctrine: (1) Puṇya-loka (meritorious world): deva-loka or svarga — attained by predominantly good karma. Enjoyable but temporary — when the merit is exhausted, the soul returns to earth (this is the pitṛyāṇa, the 'path of the fathers'). (2) Pāpa-loka (sinful world): naraka or lower realms — attained by predominantly bad karma. Painful but also temporary — when the sin is exhausted, the soul returns. (3) Manuṣya-loka (human world): rebirth as a human — attained by a mixture of puṇya and pāpa. The Gītā (6.41-45) describes this gracefully: the yogi who falls short of liberation is reborn in a family of 'the pure and prosperous' or 'the wise yogis' — a human birth with favourable conditions. The key insight: only manuṣya-loka allows new karma to be generated. In heaven and hell, the soul merely consumes past karma without creating new karma. This is why human birth is considered precious in Vedānta — it is the only state where liberation is possible, because only in the human state can one perform the conscious choice (viveka) that leads beyond karma altogether.

sk: आदित्यो ह वै बाह्यः प्राण उदयत्येष ह्येनं चाक्षुषं प्राणमनुगृह्णानः पृथिव्यां या देवता सैषा पुरुषस्यापानमवष्टभ्य अन्तरा यदाकाशः स समानो वायुर्व्यानः ||
ro: ādityaḥ · ha · vai · bāhyaḥ · prāṇaḥ · udayati · eṣaḥ · hi · enaṁ · cākṣuṣaṁ · prāṇam · anugṛhṇānaḥ · pṛthivyāṁ · yā · devatā · sā · eṣā · puruṣasya · apānam · avaṣṭabhya · antarā · yat · ākāśaḥ · saḥ · samānaḥ · vāyuḥ · vyānaḥ ||
hi: आदित्य (सूर्य) ही बाह्य प्राण है — वह उदय होता है, और चाक्षुष प्राण (नेत्रों में स्थित प्राण) को अनुग्रहित (सहायता/शक्ति प्रदान) करता है। पृथ्वी में जो देवता है — वह पुरुष के अपान को अवष्टभ्य (सहारा देकर/नियंत्रित करके) (रखती है)। बीच में जो आकाश है — वह समान (है)। वायु — (वह) व्यान (है)।
en: The sun (āditya) is indeed the external prāṇa — it rises, supporting (anugṛhṇāna) the prāṇa in the eye (cākṣuṣa prāṇa). The deity in the earth supports the apāna of the person. The space (ākāśa) between (earth and sun) is samāna. The wind (vāyu) is vyāna.

ws.e: the sun — identified as the external (bāhya) form of Prāṇa; the macrocosmic counterpart of the breath in the body
pertaining to the eye — cākṣuṣa prāṇa is the vital force that powers vision; the sun supports it by providing light

ws.h: अनुग्रह करता हुआ / सहायता करता हुआ
ws.e: supporting / favouring — anu + √grah (to seize, support); the sun 'favours' the eye-prāṇa by enabling vision through light
in between — the space between earth and sun; this intermediate zone corresponds to samāna (the 'equalising' breath in the middle zone of the body)

gr: This mantra answers the fifth sub-question: 'How does Prāṇa sustain the external (bāhyam)?' The answer maps the five internal prāṇas onto five external/cosmic counterparts: (1) Prāṇa ↔ Āditya (Sun); (2) Apāna ↔ Pṛthivī-devatā (Earth-deity); (3) Samāna ↔ Ākāśa (Space between); (4) Vyāna ↔ Vāyu (Wind); (5) Udāna ↔ Tejas/Agni (Fire — mentioned in the next mantra). This is the adhidaiva-adhyātma correspondence: every microcosmic function has a macrocosmic support. anugṛhṇānaḥ — the sun 'supports' the eye-prāṇa: without sunlight, the eye cannot see. The external and internal prāṇas are mutually dependent — the cosmic sustains the individual, and the individual participates in the cosmic.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.8 — This mantra establishes the adhidaiva-adhyātma (macrocosm-microcosm) correspondence for the five prāṇas. Compare Aitareya 1.2.4 where each sense-deity has a cosmic counterpart. The sun-eye correspondence is one of the oldest Vedic identifications — Rig Veda 1.164.14 calls the sun 'the eye of Mitra-Varuṇa'. The earth-apāna correspondence is logical: earth's gravity pulls things downward, just as apāna governs the downward-moving functions. Ākāśa-samāna: space is the 'middle' element (between earth and heaven), and samāna is the 'middle' prāṇa. Vāyu-vyāna: wind pervades the atmosphere just as vyāna pervades the body.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — बाह्य और आभ्यन्तर (external and internal) प्राण एक ही ब्रह्म की दो अभिव्यक्तियाँ हैं। सूर्य = बाह्य प्राण, श्वास = आभ्यन्तर प्राण — दोनों का स्रोत एक (आत्मा) है। यह अध्यारोप-अपवाद (superimposition and negation) विधि से समझा जाना चाहिए।
advaita.en: Shankara says the external and internal prāṇas are two expressions of one Brahman. Sun = external prāṇa, breath = internal prāṇa — both originate from one source (Ātman). This should be understood through the adhyāropa-apavāda (superimposition-negation) method.
advaita.ins: Same breath, two scales. Inside you, it powers your eyes. Outside you, it shines as the sun. The Upanishad doesn't say the sun is 'like' your breath — it says they're the same thing operating at different scales.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सूर्य, पृथ्वी, आकाश, वायु — ये सब भगवान् के शरीर (body of God) हैं। बाह्य प्राण (सूर्य) और आभ्यन्तर प्राण (श्वास) दोनों ईश्वर की शक्तियाँ हैं जो परस्पर सहयोग (cooperation) करती हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says sun, earth, space, and wind are all the Lord's body (śarīra). External prāṇa (sun) and internal prāṇa (breath) are both the Lord's powers that cooperate with each other.
vishisht.ins: The sun helps your eyes see. The earth holds your body down. Space gives your lungs room. Wind gives your blood motion. God's external body serves God's internal body. You live at the intersection.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — बाह्य-आभ्यन्तर प्राण का सम्बन्ध यह दिखाता है कि व्यक्ति (individual) और ब्रह्माण्ड (universe) एक ही चेतना-तंत्र (consciousness-system) के दो पहलू हैं। सूर्य = बाह्य ज्ञान-प्रकाश, चाक्षुष प्राण = आन्तरिक ज्ञान-शक्ति।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the connection between external and internal prāṇa shows that individual and universe are two aspects of one consciousness-system. Sun = external knowledge-light, eye-prāṇa = internal knowledge-power.
aurobindo.ins: You're not a separate being inside a separate universe. You're a localised expression of the same consciousness that shines as the sun, gravitates as the earth, expands as space, and flows as wind. Same system, different zoom level.

dp.q: 🔍 The macrocosm-microcosm correspondence
dp.a: This mantra establishes one of the most important principles in Vedic thought: the adhidaiva-adhyātma (macrocosm-microcosm) correspondence. Every internal (bodily) function has an external (cosmic) support: Internal → External: Prāṇa (breath in the nose/eyes) → Āditya (Sun); Apāna (downward breath) → Pṛthivī (Earth); Samāna (digestive breath) → Ākāśa (Space); Vyāna (circulating breath) → Vāyu (Wind); Udāna (ascending breath) → Tejas/Agni (Fire). The correspondences are not arbitrary — they follow a functional logic: Sun provides light → eye-prāṇa needs light to see. Earth's gravity pulls downward → apāna governs downward-moving functions. Space occupies the middle → samāna operates in the middle of the body. Wind pervades everywhere → vyāna pervades the entire body. Fire rises upward → udāna moves upward at death. The practical implication: the individual is not a self-contained system but is embedded in the cosmos. Your prāṇa depends on the sun; your apāna depends on the earth. You cannot separate yourself from the universe — you are woven into it. This is the basis of Vedic ecology: harming the cosmos harms the individual, because they share the same vital infrastructure.

dp.q: 🔍 How does the sun 'support' the eye?
dp.a: The phrase cākṣuṣaṁ prāṇam anugṛhṇānaḥ ('supporting the prāṇa in the eye') describes a relationship that operates on multiple levels: Physical: the sun provides light, without which the eye cannot function. Vision requires both an internal capacity (the eye-prāṇa) and an external enabler (sunlight). Neither alone produces sight. Energetic: the sun's energy (photons) is absorbed by the eye's photoreceptors and converted into neural signals. The eye-prāṇa is the vital capacity that makes this conversion possible — a dead person's eye receives light but cannot see. Metaphysical: the sun is the external manifestation of the same consciousness (Prāṇa/Ātman) that operates as the eye's internal capacity. The sun doesn't just help the eye — it is the cosmic version of the same power. This understanding persists in Hindu ritual: the Sūrya-namaskāra (sun salutation) is performed facing the sun not merely for physical health but to align the internal prāṇa with its external source. The Gāyatrī mantra invokes the sun (Savitṛ) to 'illuminate our intellects' — the same principle: the cosmic light ignites the inner light.

sk: तेजो ह वा उदानः तस्मादुपशान्ततेजाः पुनर्भवमिन्द्रियैर्मनसि सम्पद्यमानैः ||
ro: tejaḥ · ha · vā · udānaḥ · tasmāt · upaśānta-tejāḥ · punar-bhavam · indriyaiḥ · manasi · sampadyamānaiḥ ||
hi: तेज (अग्नि/ऊष्मा) ही उदान है। इसलिए जब (शरीर का) तेज उपशान्त (बुझ/शान्त) हो जाता है, तो (जीव) पुनर्भव (पुनर्जन्म) को प्राप्त होता है — इन्द्रियों के मन में सम्पद्यमान (विलीन) होने पर।
en: Fire (tejas) is indeed udāna. Therefore, when the fire (body-heat) is extinguished (upaśānta-tejas), one goes to rebirth (punar-bhava), with the senses dissolving (sampadyamāna) into the mind.

ws.e: fire / heat / lustre — tejas here is the body-heat (uṣman); udāna is identified with this fire because both move upward; the external counterpart is Agni (fire)

ws.h: जिसका तेज शान्त (बुझ) हो गया है
ws.e: one whose fire has been extinguished — upa + śānta (calmed) + tejas; describes the moment of death when body-heat ceases
rebirth / re-becoming — punaḥ (again) + bhava (becoming); the cycle of death and rebirth (saṁsāra)

ws.h: विलीन होते हुए / एकत्र होते हुए
ws.e: dissolving / merging — sam + √pad (to go into); the senses merge into the mind at death, and the mind carries them into the next birth

gr: tejaḥ udānaḥ — 'fire is udāna': this completes the five-fold external correspondence: Prāṇa = Sun, Apāna = Earth, Samāna = Space, Vyāna = Wind, Udāna = Fire. Fire naturally rises (like udāna), and body-heat is the visible sign of udāna's presence. upaśānta-tejāḥ → punar-bhavam — 'when the fire is extinguished → rebirth': the death-process in sequence: (1) body-heat (tejas/udāna) ceases; (2) the senses (indriyas) withdraw from their objects and merge into the mind (manas); (3) the mind, carrying the senses and saṁskāras, departs for rebirth. indriyaiḥ manasi sampadyamānaiḥ — 'with the senses dissolving into the mind': at death, the five senses don't just 'switch off' — they are absorbed into manas, which carries them forward. This is why the next birth has the same faculties — they were preserved in the mind.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.9 — The death-process described here — fire-extinction → sense-withdrawal → mind-absorption → rebirth — is elaborated in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.1-6 and Kaṭha 2.3.15. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka version adds: 'speech merges into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into fire, fire into the supreme deity.' The identification of udāna with tejas (fire) is also found in Maitri Upanishad 2.6. The concept that the senses merge into the mind (not simply ceasing to function) is critical to the karma-rebirth doctrine: the mind retains the impressions of the senses and carries them to the next birth.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'इन्द्रियैः मनसि सम्पद्यमानैः' — मृत्यु के समय इन्द्रियाँ मन में विलीन होती हैं, मन प्राण में, प्राण तेज में, तेज आत्मा में। यह प्रतिलोम-क्रम (reverse order) सृष्टि के क्रम का उलटा है। ज्ञानी के लिए यह विलय मोक्ष है; अज्ञानी के लिए पुनर्भव (rebirth)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'indriyaiḥ manasi sampadyamānaiḥ' — at death, the senses dissolve into the mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into fire, fire into Ātman. This reverse order inverts the order of creation. For the knower (jñānī), this dissolution is liberation; for the ignorant, it is rebirth.
advaita.ins: Death is creation running backward. The senses fold into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into the fire, the fire into the source. The question is: do you know the source? If yes, you arrive home. If no, the journey starts again.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — पुनर्भव (rebirth) तब तक होता है जब तक जीव भगवान् को नहीं जानता। 'उपशान्ततेजाः' — शरीर की अग्नि बुझना = भगवान् का उस शरीर से हटना। जब भगवान् नया शरीर चुनते हैं, तब इन्द्रियाँ मन के साथ वहाँ पहुँचती हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says rebirth continues until the jīva knows the Lord. 'Upaśānta-tejas' — body-fire extinguishing = the Lord withdrawing from that body. When the Lord selects a new body, the senses arrive there with the mind.
vishisht.ins: The fire doesn't go out randomly. The Lord leaves, and the fire follows. When He enters a new body, the fire lights again. You think you're dying — actually, the Lord is relocating.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'तेजः उदानः' — उदान चेतना की ऊर्ध्वगामी अग्नि है। जब यह अग्नि बुझती है, तो चेतना एक स्तर नीचे गिरती है — इन्द्रियाँ मन में, मन अवचेतन (subconscient) में। पुनर्जन्म = चेतना का पुनः बाहरी प्रकटीकरण।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'tejaḥ udānaḥ' — udāna is the ascending fire of consciousness. When this fire goes out, consciousness falls one level — senses into mind, mind into the subconscient. Rebirth is consciousness manifesting outward again.
aurobindo.ins: Death isn't an end — it's a contraction. Consciousness pulls inward, the senses fold into the mind, the mind goes dark. And then, from that darkness, it unfolds again in a new form. The fire doesn't die — it relocates.

dp.q: 🔍 The Vedāntic process of death
dp.a: The Upanishads describe death as a sequential withdrawal (pratiloma-krama, 'reverse order') of the faculties: Step 1: The five senses (jñānendriyas) withdraw from their objects and merge into the mind (manas). Sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell cease — but the mind still functions (hence dying persons may have mental activity even after sensory shutdown). Step 2: The mind merges into prāṇa (the vital breath). Mental activity ceases, but the breath continues briefly. Step 3: Prāṇa merges into tejas (body-heat/udāna). The breath stops, but residual warmth remains in the body. Step 4: Tejas merges into the Ātman (or into the subtle body that departs). Body-heat ceases — the body is now clinically dead. This process is described in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.1-2: 'The tip of the heart lights up; by that light the Self departs...' and Chāndogya 6.15.1-2: 'Speech merges into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into fire, fire into the supreme deity.' The key point: the senses don't simply vanish at death — they are preserved within the mind, which is preserved within the prāṇa, which departs as the subtle body. This is how the faculties are 'carried' to the next birth: they travel as potentials (saṁskāras) within the departing mind-prāṇa complex.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is fire (tejas) identified with udāna?
dp.a: The identification of udāna with tejas (fire) rests on several correspondences: (1) Direction: fire naturally rises (flames point upward). Udāna is the upward-moving breath. Both share the quality of ūrdhva-gati (ascending motion). (2) Visible sign: body-heat (uṣman) is the visible sign of udāna's presence. When a person is alive, the body is warm — when udāna departs, the body cools. The extinction of body-heat (upaśānta-tejas) is the medical sign of death. (3) Speech: speech (vāk) is powered by udāna (throat region) and is also associated with Agni (Fire) in Vedic thought — Agni is the deity of speech (Aitareya 1.2.4). (4) Ascent at death: fire carries offerings upward to the gods (havya-vāhana); udāna carries the jīva upward at death. Both are vehicles of ascent. (5) Cosmic fire: in the external-internal correspondence (mantra 8), all four other prāṇas were matched to cosmic elements (sun, earth, space, wind). Udāna = fire completes the set, mapping all five prāṇas to the pañca-mahābhūta (five great elements) of Sāṅkhya: Prāṇa-Sun (light), Apāna-Earth, Samāna-Space, Vyāna-Wind, Udāna-Fire.

sk: यच्चित्तस्तेनैष प्राणमायाति प्राणस्तेजसा युक्तः सहात्मना यथासङ्कल्पितं लोकं नयति ||
ro: yat · cittaḥ · tena · eṣaḥ · prāṇam · āyāti · prāṇaḥ · tejasā · yuktaḥ · saha · ātmanā · yathā-saṅkalpitaṁ · lokaṁ · nayati ||
hi: जो (जीव) चित्त (मन/ज्ञान) से युक्त है, वह (मन के साथ) प्राण में आता है (मिलता है)। प्राण, तेज (उदान/अग्नि) से युक्त होकर, आत्मा (जीवात्मा) सहित, यथा-संकल्पित (जैसा मन ने संकल्प/इच्छा किया है उसके अनुसार) लोक में ले जाता है।
en: Whatever is in the mind (citta), by that one comes to Prāṇa. Prāṇa, united with fire (tejas/udāna), together with the individual self (ātman), leads (the departing soul) to whatever world was willed (yathā-saṅkalpita).

ws.h: चित्त / मन / अन्तःकरण में जो विचार-संस्कार हैं
ws.e: mind / consciousness / the totality of mental impressions — citta here includes all accumulated thoughts, desires, and saṁskāras

ws.h: जैसा संकल्प (इच्छा/निश्चय) किया है उसके अनुसार
ws.e: as willed / as determined by one's resolve — yathā (as) + saṅkalpita (resolved/intended); the mind's dominant intention at death determines the destination
with fire — instrumental of tejas; prāṇa is 'fuelled' by the fire of udāna for the upward journey
world / realm / destination — the world to which the departing jīva is carried

gr: yac-cittaḥ tena prāṇam āyāti — 'whatever is in the mind, by that one comes to Prāṇa': at death, the mind's contents (last thought, dominant desire, accumulated saṁskāras) merge into prāṇa and determine the direction of departure. yathā-saṅkalpitaṁ lokam — 'to the world as willed/resolved': the destination is not random but saṅkalpa-determined. The Gītā (8.6) makes this explicit: 'yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajaty ante kalevaram / taṁ tam evaiti' — 'whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that state one goes.' prāṇaḥ tejasā yuktaḥ saha ātmanā — a three-part vehicle: Prāṇa (the engine), tejas/udāna (the fuel), and ātman (the passenger). The departing soul is not naked — it travels in a subtle vehicle composed of mind, prāṇa, and fire.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.10 — The doctrine that the mind's last thought/intention determines the afterlife destination is shared across Indian traditions: Gītā 8.6, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.5 ('as is one's desire, so is one's will; as one's will, so one's deed; as one's deed, so what one attains'). The concept of saṅkalpa (resolve/intention) as the determining factor in rebirth bridges the Upanishadic karma-doctrine with Buddhist kamma-theory, where cetanā (intention) is identified with karma itself. The three-part vehicle (prāṇa + tejas + ātman) corresponds to the sūkṣma-śarīra (subtle body) of later Vedānta: the liṅga-śarīra composed of the five prāṇas, five jñānendriyas, five karmendriyas, manas, buddhi, ahaṁkāra, and citta.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'यथासंकल्पित' — जीव जिस लोक की कामना (desire) करता है, मृत्यु-काल में वही संकल्प प्रबल होता है, और प्राण उसी लोक में ले जाता है। ज्ञानी का संकल्प 'ब्रह्म' है — इसलिए वह ब्रह्म को ही प्राप्त करता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'yathā-saṅkalpita' — the jīva's dominant desire at death determines the world it reaches. The jñānī's saṅkalpa is 'Brahman' — therefore he attains Brahman alone.
advaita.ins: Your last thought is your boarding pass. A lifetime of desires condenses into one final intention — and Prāṇa flies you to that destination. This is why the Upanishads say: practice thinking of Brahman now, so that when the moment comes, that thought is the one that surfaces.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सहात्मना' — भगवान् (अन्तर्यामी) जीव के साथ ही जाते हैं। 'यथासंकल्पित' — भगवान् जीव के संकल्प और कर्म के अनुसार उचित लोक का चयन करते हैं। भक्त का अन्तिम संकल्प 'भगवान्' ही होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'saha ātmanā' — the Lord (as antaryāmī, inner ruler) accompanies the jīva. 'Yathā-saṅkalpita' — the Lord selects the appropriate world based on the jīva's saṅkalpa and karma. The devotee's last saṅkalpa is 'the Lord' — and the Lord takes him personally.
vishisht.ins: You don't travel alone at death. The Lord goes with you — 'saha ātmanā'. He's not the judge waiting at the gate; He's the companion on the journey. And for the devotee, the journey ends at His feet.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'यथासंकल्पित' — चेतना अपना अगला क्षेत्र (field) स्वयं चुनती है। संकल्प = चेतना की गुणवत्ता (quality) — जीवन में जो चेतना विकसित (developed) की, मृत्यु में वही दिशा निर्धारित करती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'yathā-saṅkalpita' — consciousness chooses its next field of operation. Saṅkalpa = the quality of consciousness — the consciousness developed during life determines the direction at death.
aurobindo.ins: You don't 'go' somewhere at death. Your consciousness gravitates to the level it has reached. A water-seeker doesn't choose the river — gravity takes him there. Similarly, the quality of your consciousness finds its own level.

dp.q: 🔍 How does the 'last thought' determine rebirth?
dp.a: The doctrine of yathā-saṅkalpita ('as willed/intended') is one of the most practically important teachings in the Upanishads. It states that the mind's dominant content at death determines the next birth. This operates through several mechanisms: (1) Last-moment thought: the Gītā (8.6) states explicitly: 'Whatever state one remembers at the moment of leaving the body, to that state one goes, O Kaunteya, being always shaped by that state.' If you think of God at death, you go to God. If you think of your wealth, you return to pursue it. (2) Not arbitrary: the last thought is not random — it is the summary of a lifetime of mental habits. A person who has spent decades thinking about money will naturally think about money at death. A person who has practiced God-meditation will naturally think of God. (3) Saṅkalpa as karma: saṅkalpa (resolve/intention) is not just a wish — it is the active force of karma. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.5) chain is: desire → will → deed → attainment. The saṅkalpa at death is the concentrated force of all prior desires. Practical implication: this is why the tradition recommends continuous God-remembrance (smaraṇa) during life — so that at the critical moment, the divine name surfaces naturally. The famous story of Ajāmila (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1-3) illustrates this: a sinner who called his son's name 'Nārāyaṇa' at death was saved because the divine name was on his lips.

dp.q: 🔍 The 'subtle vehicle' of the departing soul
dp.a: The mantra describes the departing soul's three-component vehicle: (1) Prāṇa — the engine that propels the journey. The life-force doesn't simply vanish at death; it carries the jīva to the next destination. (2) Tejas (fire/udāna) — the fuel. Udāna is the upward-moving force that lifts consciousness out of the body. It is 'united with' (yukta) prāṇa, providing the energy for departure. (3) Ātman (the individual self) — the passenger. The jīvātman, carrying its saṁskāras (impressions) and karma, rides this vehicle to its next embodiment. This three-part vehicle corresponds to what later Vedānta calls the sūkṣma-śarīra (subtle body) or liṅga-śarīra (marker-body). This subtle body consists of: the five prāṇas, the five sense-capacities (not the physical organs), the five action-capacities, manas (mind), buddhi (intellect), ahaṁkāra (ego), and citta (memory/impression-store). The subtle body persists across births — it is the vehicle of transmigration. Only when final liberation (mokṣa) is attained does the subtle body dissolve, and the Ātman stands free.

sk: य एवं विद्वान्प्राणं वेद न हास्य प्रजा हीयते ऽमृतो भवति तदेषः श्लोकः ||
ro: yaḥ · evaṁ · vidvān · prāṇaṁ · veda · na · ha · asya · prajā · hīyate · amṛtaḥ · bhavati · tat · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ ||
hi: जो इस प्रकार (एवम्) जानकर (विद्वान्) प्राण को जानता है — उसकी प्रजा (सन्तान/रचना) क्षीण नहीं होती, और वह अमृत (मृत्युरहित/अविनाशी) हो जाता है। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: He who, knowing thus, knows Prāṇa — his offspring (prajā) does not perish, and he becomes immortal (amṛta). On this there is this verse (śloka) —

ws.e: the knower — one who knows with full understanding (not mere information but direct realisation); from √vid (to know)
offspring / progeny / creation — can mean biological offspring (his lineage continues) or metaphysical creation (his works endure)

ws.h: क्षीण होती है / नष्ट होती है
ws.e: perishes / diminishes — √hā (to leave, diminish); passive: 'is not diminished'
immortal — a (not) + mṛta (dead); the knower of Prāṇa transcends death
verse — a metrical composition; Pippalāda introduces a concluding verse to summarise the teaching

gr: evaṁ vidvān — 'knowing thus': the evaṁ is critical — it means 'in this manner', referring to the entire teaching of Question 3 (origin from Ātman, shadow-simile, fivefold division, nāḍī-system, departure mechanism). Mere intellectual knowledge is not sufficient; one must know in this specific manner — with full understanding of the cause, mechanism, and implications. na prajā hīyate — 'his offspring does not perish': the Vedic blessing of continuity — not just biological reproduction but the endurance of one's works, lineage, and spiritual legacy. amṛto bhavati — 'he becomes immortal': the ultimate fruit of prāṇa-vidyā. By knowing the source of Prāṇa (Ātman), the knower identifies with the source itself — and the source is deathless. eṣaḥ ślokaḥ — 'there is this verse': a formulaic transition to a summary verse, common in Upanishadic prose-verse structure.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.11 — The phala-śruti (declaration of the fruit of knowledge) follows a standard pattern: 'he who knows this becomes X.' Compare Chāndogya 1.1.10: 'He who knows this — whatever he desires, that desire is fulfilled.' The promise of immortality through knowledge is the central promise of all Upanishads: knowledge of the Self = liberation from death. The next mantra (3.12) provides the concluding verse.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'एवं विद्वान्' — जो प्राण को इस प्रकार जानता है — अर्थात् 'आत्मनः जायते' (आत्मा से उत्पन्न होता है) — वह आत्मा को ही जान लेता है, और आत्म-ज्ञानी मृत्यु से परे हो जाता है। 'अमृतः' — यह जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while alive) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'evaṁ vidvān' — who knows Prāṇa 'in this manner' — meaning 'born from Ātman' — knows the Ātman itself, and the knower of Ātman transcends death. 'Amṛta' — this is jīvanmukti (liberation while still alive).
advaita.ins: Knowing the breath isn't biology — it's metaphysics. When you know that your breath comes from the Self, you've just learned that you are the Self. And the Self doesn't die. That's the trick: follow the breath to its source, and you find immortality.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'प्राणं वेद' — जो प्राण को भगवान् की शक्ति (power of God) के रूप में जानता है, वह भगवान् को ही जानता है। 'अमृतः' — ऐसा भक्त भगवान् के परम धाम (supreme abode) को प्राप्त करता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'prāṇaṁ veda' — who knows Prāṇa as the Lord's power knows the Lord Himself. 'Amṛta' — such a devotee attains the Lord's supreme abode.
vishisht.ins: You don't need to know everything about God. Just know one thing deeply enough — even the breath — and follow it to its source. At the source, you find the Lord. And the Lord's abode is deathless.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अमृतो भवति' — यह शारीरिक अमरता नहीं, अपितु चेतना की अमरता है। जो प्राण के स्रोत (आत्मा) को जानता है, वह जान लेता है कि चेतना अविनाशी है — शरीर बदलता है, चेतना नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'amṛto bhavati' is not physical immortality but immortality of consciousness. Who knows the source of Prāṇa (Ātman) realises that consciousness is indestructible — bodies change, consciousness does not.
aurobindo.ins: Immortality isn't living forever in one body. It's knowing that you are not the body. The breath comes from the Self; the Self doesn't die. Know the source, and death becomes a change of clothes, not an ending.

dp.q: 🔍 What is 'prāṇa-vidyā' and its fruit?
dp.a: Prāṇa-vidyā (knowledge of Prāṇa) is one of the major meditation-disciplines (upāsanās) described in the Upanishads. Its components, as taught in Question 3, are: (1) Knowing Prāṇa's origin — from the Ātman (not from matter). (2) Knowing its mechanism — fivefold division, nāḍī-system, macrocosm-microcosm correspondence. (3) Knowing its departure — through udāna, determined by saṅkalpa and karma. The fruit (phala) is twofold: (a) na prajā hīyate — 'offspring does not perish': this is the Vedic blessing of continuity. At the practical level, it means the knower's lineage and legacy endure. At the deeper level, it means the knower's spiritual creation (his knowledge-transmission) continues through his students. (b) amṛto bhavati — 'he becomes immortal': the supreme fruit. By knowing that Prāṇa originates from the deathless Ātman, the knower identifies with the Ātman — and the Ātman is by definition amṛta (deathless). This is not a future event ('he will become immortal after death') but a present realisation ('he is immortal, right now, because he knows his true nature'). In Advaita terms, this is jīvanmukti — liberation while still embodied.

dp.q: 🔍 The phala-śruti tradition
dp.a: The phala-śruti (फलश्रुति, 'declaration of fruit') is a standard Upanishadic formula that states the benefit of a particular knowledge or practice. It typically follows the pattern: 'yaḥ evaṁ veda... amṛto bhavati' — 'he who knows this thus... becomes immortal.' Examples across the Upanishads: Chāndogya 1.1.10: 'He who meditates on OM with this knowledge — whatever he desires, that is fulfilled.' Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10: 'He who knows "I am Brahman" — he becomes this All.'
