Kaṭha 2.3.18: 'Nachiketa, having gained this knowledge and the entire yoga-teaching from Death, attained Brahman and became free from passion and death.' The phala-śruti serves several functions: (1) Motivation: it incentivises the student to pursue the knowledge with full commitment. (2) Validation: it confirms that this knowledge leads to the highest goal (mokṣa). (3) Discrimination: it distinguishes between lower knowledge (which yields worldly fruits) and higher knowledge (which yields immortality). The promise of amṛtatva (immortality) is reserved for the highest knowledge — knowledge of the Self.

sk: उत्पत्तिमायतिं स्थानं विभुत्वं चैव पञ्चधा अध्यात्मं चैव प्राणस्य विज्ञायामृतमश्नुते विज्ञायामृतमश्नुत इति ||
ro: utpattim · āyatiṁ · sthānaṁ · vibhutvaṁ · ca · eva · pañcadhā · adhyātmaṁ · ca · eva · prāṇasya · vijñāya · amṛtam · aśnute · vijñāya · amṛtam · aśnute · iti ||
hi: प्राण की उत्पत्ति (origin), आयति (प्रवेश-मार्ग), स्थान (seat/position), पंचधा विभुत्व (पाँच रूपों में विस्तार), और अध्यात्म (आन्तरिक स्वरूप) — इन सबको विज्ञाय (ठीक से जानकर), (जीव) अमृत को अश्नुते (प्राप्त करता है)। अमृत को प्राप्त करता है। — इति (इस प्रकार तीसरा प्रश्न समाप्त)।
en: Having known (vijñāya) the origin (utpatti), the entry (āyati), the seat (sthāna), the fivefold sovereignty (vibhutva pañcadhā), and the internal nature (adhyātma) of Prāṇa — one attains immortality (amṛtam aśnute). One attains immortality. — Thus (ends the third question).

ws.e: origin — from Ātman (mantra 3)
entry / coming — how Prāṇa enters the body through mano-kṛtena (mantra 3)
seat / station — the stations of the five prāṇas in the body (mantras 5-6)
sovereignty / all-pervasiveness — vibhu (sovereign, all-pervading); the cosmic scope of Prāṇa

ws.h: पाँच प्रकार से / पाँच रूपों में
ws.e: fivefold — the five forms of Prāṇa (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna)
attains / reaches — √aś (to attain, pervade); the knower reaches the state of immortality

gr: Five aspects of prāṇa-vidyā summarised: (1) utpatti — origin (from Ātman, mantra 3); (2) āyati — entry into the body (by mano-kṛtena, mantra 3); (3) sthāna — stations/seats (the five territories, mantras 5-6); (4) vibhutva pañcadhā — fivefold sovereignty (the five prāṇas and their cosmic correspondences, mantras 5-9); (5) adhyātma — internal nature (the nāḍī-system, heart-seat of Ātman, death-mechanism, mantras 6-10). vijñāya amṛtam aśnute — 'having known, one attains immortality': the verse repeats this phrase twice for emphasis — a common Upanishadic rhetorical device (cf. Kaṭha 2.3.18 double ending). The repetition of vijñāya amṛtam aśnute closes the third question with the same promise that opened it: the reward for this knowledge is deathlessness. iti — 'thus': marks the formal conclusion of Question 3.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_3.12 — The concluding verse neatly summarises the five aspects of prāṇa-vidyā taught in Question 3, mapping them back to Kausalya's original six sub-questions (mantra 1). The double repetition of 'vijñāya amṛtam aśnute' is a common Upanishadic closing device — it serves as a seal (mudrā) on the teaching. Compare Muṇḍaka 3.2.9: 'sa yo ha vai tat paramaṁ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati' — 'he who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman indeed' — repeated for emphasis. The five-term summary (utpatti, āyati, sthāna, vibhutva, adhyātma) provides a study-guide for meditation: the practitioner should contemplate each aspect sequentially.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — ये पाँच विषय (origin, entry, station, fivefold sovereignty, inner nature) प्राण-विद्या के पाँच चरण (stages) हैं। इन्हें क्रमशः ध्यान (meditate) करना चाहिए। 'अमृतमश्नुते' — यह जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while alive) है; शारीरिक मृत्यु पर ब्रह्म-प्राप्ति (videha-mukti) होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says these five topics (origin, entry, station, fivefold sovereignty, inner nature) are five stages of prāṇa-vidyā. They should be meditated upon sequentially. 'Amṛtam aśnute' is jīvanmukti (liberation while alive); at physical death, videha-mukti (bodiless liberation) follows.
advaita.ins: Five steps to immortality: know where Prāṇa comes from, how it enters, where it sits, how it rules, and what it is inside. Each step takes you deeper. At the end, you find — you were the source all along.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण-विद्या ईश्वर-ज्ञान का एक मार्ग है। प्राण के पाँच पहलुओं को जानना = ईश्वर की पाँच विभूतियों (glories) को जानना। 'अमृतम्' = ईश्वर का परमधाम, जहाँ पुनर्जन्म नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says prāṇa-vidyā is a path to God-knowledge. Knowing Prāṇa's five aspects = knowing five of the Lord's vibhūtis. 'Amṛtam' = the Lord's supreme abode, from which there is no return.
vishisht.ins: Five windows into God's nature. Through each window you see a different aspect of the divine engineer — how He creates life, how He enters it, how He distributes it, how He rules it, and what He looks like from inside. See through all five, and you never need to look back.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण-विद्या के पाँच पहलू चेतना के क्रमिक अनावरण (progressive unveiling) के चरण हैं। 'अमृतमश्नुते' — चेतना अपने अमर स्रोत को पहचान लेती है; यही 'अमृत-प्राप्ति' है — न कोई 'लोक' जाना, न कोई 'पुरस्कार' — केवल पहचान (recognition)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the five aspects of prāṇa-vidyā are stages of the progressive unveiling of consciousness. 'Amṛtam aśnute' — consciousness recognises its own immortal source; this is the 'attainment of immortality' — not going to any 'world' or receiving any 'reward' but simply recognition.
aurobindo.ins: Immortality isn't a prize you win. It's a fact you recognise. The five steps of prāṇa-vidyā don't take you somewhere new — they strip away the five layers of ignorance until you see what was always there: the deathless source.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Question 3 answer all six sub-questions?
dp.a: Kausalya asked six sub-questions (mantra 1). The concluding verse (mantra 12) maps the five-term summary back to those questions: (1) 'Whence is Prāṇa born?' → utpatti (origin) — from the Ātman, like a shadow from a person (mantra 3). (2) 'How does it enter the body?' → āyati (entry) — by mano-kṛtena, through the mind's past karma (mantra 3). (3) 'How does it establish itself after division?' → sthāna (station) — five prāṇas assigned to five body-zones (mantras 4-5). (4) 'By what does it depart?' → vibhutva pañcadhā (fivefold sovereignty) includes the departure mechanism: udāna exits through suṣumnā, carrying the jīva according to karma (mantras 7, 9-10). (5) 'How does it sustain the external?' → the cosmic correspondences: sun, earth, space, wind, fire (mantra 8). (6) 'How does it sustain the internal?' → adhyātma (internal nature) — the nāḍī-system, the heart-seat of the Ātman, vyāna's circulation (mantra 6). All six questions are answered, and the five-term summary provides a complete study-guide for meditation on Prāṇa.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the promise of immortality repeated twice?
dp.a: The double repetition of vijñāya amṛtam aśnute ('having known, one attains immortality') is a deliberate Upanishadic rhetorical device with several functions: (1) Emphasis: repetition drives home the supreme importance of the teaching. This is not ordinary knowledge — it confers amṛtatva (deathlessness). (2) Closure: the repeated phrase acts as a colophon — a seal marking the end of the question. The listener knows the teaching is complete. (3) Meditation-seed: the repeated phrase is meant to be memorised and recited as a meditation formula. The student takes this phrase away and repeats it internally, reinforcing the knowledge. (4) Vedic convention: many Upanishadic sections end with doubled phrases. The Kaṭha Upanishad (2.3.18) ends similarly: 'Having received this knowledge given by Death, and the entire yoga-teaching, Nachiketa attained Brahman and became free from passion and death — and so may anyone who knows this concerning the Self.' The repetition transforms a teaching into a promise — the Upanishad is saying: this is guaranteed. Know this, and immortality is yours. Know this, and immortality is yours.
